kzz7yh-a02943-d1e103.summary: Literal glosses on the opening of Lombard's prologue: 'penuria' signifies the lack of acquired knowledge and 'tenuitas' the lack of natural intelligence; the 'gazophylacium' is etymologized and distinguished from corbona and musach; 'ardua scandere' is read as a threefold ascent (leaving sensible species, imaginative phantasms, and the resistance of natural reasons); 'praesumpsimus' is taken as good confidence in God's aid rather than arrogance; the Samaritan, the half-dead man, and the two denarii are allegorized as Christ, fallen humanity, and the two Testaments; 'supererogating' raises the objection of Apocalypse 22 against adding to Scripture.
claims: Penuria signifies lack of acquired knowledge, tenuitas lack of natural intelligence.
Good presumption is confidence in God's special help, not self-reliance.
The two denarii of the Samaritan signify the Old and New Testaments.

kzz7yh-a02943-d1e173.summary: Resolves the objection from Apocalypse 22: one may not add anything dissimilar or contrary to Scripture, but one may add truth that explains it, which is not properly adding but making explicit what is implicitly and virtually contained there. Further glosses: 'zeal for God's house' excludes evil but not good fellowship; the 'carnal' imagine God with bodily members and the 'animal' with soulish affections; the 'tower of David' is Scripture, founded on the literal sense with the moral, allegorical, and anagogical senses rising above; the 'shields' are reasons, examples, and authorities; the 'biga' is tongue and pen moved by love of God and neighbor.
claims: Theological exposition does not add to Scripture but makes explicit what it implicitly contains.
The literal sense is the foundation of Scripture, with moral, allegorical, and anagogical senses built upon it.

kzz7yh-a02943-d1e215.summary: Opening (corrupt) resolves a difficulty by holding that something cannot be known except by revelation, though it can be conjectured, which is probable opinion rather than knowledge. Further glosses: a calumniator is an accuser of a false crime; dissenting judgment follows the will because the will strongly draws the judgment; truth goes un-understood for three reasons, analogous to the three impediments of sight: a defect in the cognitive power, aversion from the truth, or a diminution of the influence of uncreated light owing to sin.
claims: Conjecture about what is known only by revelation is opinion, not knowledge.
Truth is not understood through cognitive defect, aversion, or sin-diminished divine illumination.

kzz7yh-a02943-d1e259.summary: Objection (opening corrupt) against Lombard's language of hating truth: all humans by nature desire to know, and only the true is known, so all humans naturally love truth.

kzz7yh-a02943-d1e276.summary: Reply: truth as such cannot be hated, since it is the intellect's perfection and every thing naturally desires its perfection; but it can be hated accidentally, as punishing or reproving, as Augustine says the wicked love truth shining but hate it reproving; this explains Augustine's homily on Herod and John the Baptist. Remaining glosses explain 'obnitatur', superstition's appearance of wisdom, mendacious hypocrisy, 'pruriginem', 'opilare', 'viperine doctrine' as heretical, and the 'free corrector' who corrects out of love not envy.
claims: Truth cannot be hated per se because it is the good of the intellect.
Truth can be hated per accidens as reproving or punishing.
A true corrector reproves out of love, not envy.

kzz7yh-a02943.summary: Circa litteram on Lombard's prologue: a run of literal and allegorical glosses on key words, interspersed with two short disputed points. Richard explains Lombard's self-description ('penuria', 'tenuitas'), the allegory of the Good Samaritan, and the metaphors of the tower of David (Scripture with its four senses) and the biga. He resolves the worry that commentary adds to Scripture by holding that exposition only makes explicit what Scripture implicitly contains. He also analyzes why truth goes unrecognized and argues that truth, as the good of the intellect, cannot be hated per se but only per accidens, as reproving.
claims: Exposition of Scripture makes explicit what is implicit and does not add to it.
Truth can be hated only accidentally, as reproving.
Scripture's literal sense is the foundation for its spiritual senses.
